questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days. Regional lymph nodes are firm and non-tender. Darkfield microscopy shows spiral-shaped organisms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Primary syphilis presents as a painless, indurated (hard) chancre with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy. Darkfield microscopy demonstrating Treponema pallidum (spiral-shaped) confirms the diagnosis. Chancroid produces painful ulcers; herpes produces vesicles/painful ulcers.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a non-healing ulcer on the dorsum of right hand for 6 months. The ulcer has a 'wash leather' base with violaceous undermined edges. Biopsy shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with giant cells and sulfur granules. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Actinomycosis is a bacterial (Actinomyces israelii) infection presenting with indurated swelling, sinus tracts, and characteristic 'sulfur granules' (yellow colonies of bacteria). The gram-positive filamentous bacteria form these granules visible on histology and in discharge.

questions.q: A 45-year-old immunocompetent patient presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base following a dermatomal distribution on the right thorax. One week later, severe burning pain persists even after vesicles have healed. What is the most appropriate management for the persisting pain?
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the persistent pain after herpes zoster healing. First-line treatment includes tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), gabapentinoids (gabapentin/pregabalin), and topical lidocaine patches. Antivirals have no role once lesions have healed.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on the trunk. Slit skin smear shows acid-fast bacilli. Nerve thickening is noted. Histopathology shows foamy macrophages laden with bacilli (globi) with no lymphocytic response. What type of leprosy does this represent?
questions.exp: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) is the anergic pole of the spectrum. Histology shows foamy (Virchow) macrophages filled with AFB (globi), with absent lymphocytic response, reflecting absent cell-mediated immunity. Skin smear is strongly positive (BI 5-6+). Tuberculoid shows well-formed granulomas with lymphocytes.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman on treatment for leprosy develops acute erythematous tender nodules on the face and extremities, along with fever and arthralgia. Her nerve function is intact. What is the most likely reaction and appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL/Type 2 reaction) presents with tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic symptoms. It occurs in LL/BL leprosy and is immune-complex mediated. Thalidomide is the drug of choice for ENL in males. Corticosteroids are used when thalidomide is contraindicated. Type 1 (reversal) reaction is treated with prednisolone.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with well-defined scaly plaques on the scalp, with broken-off hair shafts and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. KOH mount shows spores inside (endothrix) the hair shaft. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Endothrix tinea capitis (hair shaft invasion with spores inside) is caused by Trichophyton tonsurans and T. violaceum. T. violaceum causes black dot ringworm where broken hair stubs appear as black dots. Microsporum causes ectothrix infection. E. floccosum does not invade hair.

questions.q: A 40-year-old diabetic presents with rapidly spreading cellulitis of the scrotum with crepitus and blackish necrosis. There is severe systemic toxicity. What is this condition and what is the definitive treatment?
questions.exp: Fournier's gangrene is a polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum/genitalia, more common in diabetics and immunocompromised. Crepitus indicates gas-forming organisms. Definitive treatment is aggressive surgical debridement along with broad-spectrum antibiotics. High mortality if untreated.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and arthralgia. ANA is positive (1:640), anti-dsDNA is elevated, and complement (C3/C4) levels are low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: SLE criteria include malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthritis, positive ANA, elevated anti-dsDNA (specific for SLE), and low complement levels indicating active disease with immune complex consumption. Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE and correlates with disease activity/lupus nephritis.

questions.q: A 60-year-old presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash on eyelids, and Gottron papules on knuckles. CPK is markedly elevated. What is the most important investigation to perform next?
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis in adults over 40 is strongly associated with underlying malignancy (20-25% cases), most commonly ovarian, lung, GI, and breast cancer. Malignancy workup is mandatory in all adult dermatomyositis patients. The heliotrope rash and Gottron papules are pathognomonic of dermatomyositis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old presents with tense blisters on the trunk and limbs. Biopsy shows subepidermal blister with eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. ELISA shows antibodies against BP180. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense subepidermal blisters (intact roof due to subepidermal split), eosinophilia, and autoantibodies against BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230 at the DEJ. DIF shows linear IgG/C3. In contrast, pemphigus shows intraepidermal blisters with antibodies against desmogleins.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters on the oral mucosa and skin. Blisters rupture easily leaving erosions. Tzanck smear shows acantholytic cells. DIF shows intercellular IgG deposits in a 'chicken-wire' pattern. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris presents with flaccid intraepidermal blisters, positive Nikolsky sign, and acantholytic cells on Tzanck smear. Antibodies against desmoglein 3 (mucosal) and desmoglein 1 (cutaneous). First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone), often combined with steroid-sparing agents like azathioprine or rituximab.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on extensor elbows, knees, and buttocks. Skin biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at the dermal papillae tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the DEJ. He also has malabsorption symptoms. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease). It presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces. Pathology shows neutrophilic microabscesses at papillary tips. DIF shows granular IgA at DEJ (pathognomonic). Treatment: gluten-free diet + dapsone.

questions.q: A 68-year-old presents with a pearly, telangiectatic nodule with rolled edges on the nose. It has been slowly enlarging over 2 years. Biopsy shows basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and cleft artifact. What is the appropriate management?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose (H-zone of face) requires Mohs micrographic surgery for maximum tissue conservation and the highest cure rate. Mohs surgery allows real-time margin control and is indicated for high-risk locations (face), recurrent tumors, and morpheaform variants. BCC shows peripheral palisading of basaloid cells with stromal retraction (cleft artifact).

questions.q: A 55-year-old farmer presents with an indurated nodule on the lower lip that has been enlarging for 6 months. It bleeds on touch. Cervical lymph nodes are palpable. Biopsy shows keratin pearls and dyskeratotic cells. What is the correct statement regarding this tumor?
opts: It is more common on the upper lip
Sun exposure is NOT a risk factor
Metastasis risk is higher than BCC
Peripheral palisading is characteristic on histology
questions.exp: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lip is more common on the lower lip (sun-exposed). SCC has a significantly higher metastatic potential than BCC (2-3% for BCC vs 2-10% overall for SCC, with lip SCC having ~10-15% risk). Histology shows keratin pearls and dyskeratotic cells. Peripheral palisading is a feature of BCC, not SCC.

questions.q: A 30-year-old presents with a rapidly growing, reddish-brown plaque on the back with satellite lesions. Biopsy shows spindle-shaped cells with storiform pattern and prominent CD34 positivity. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: DFSP presents as a slow-growing, locally aggressive fibrosarcoma with low metastatic potential. It shows storiform (cartwheel) pattern of spindle cells. CD34 positivity is a hallmark (helps differentiate from dermatofibroma which is CD34 negative). It has characteristic t(17;22) translocation creating COL1A1-PDGFB fusion. Imatinib is used for unresectable cases.

questions.q: A 65-year-old presents with a 2cm asymmetric lesion on the back with irregular borders and variegated color (black, brown, red). ABCDE criteria are met. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is positive. Breslow thickness is 2.5mm with ulceration. What is the T stage?
questions.exp: Melanoma T staging (AJCC 8th edition): T3 = Breslow thickness >2.0-4.0mm. 'b' suffix denotes ulceration. Therefore, 2.5mm thickness with ulceration = T3b. Ulceration worsens prognosis and upstages the tumor. Positive SLNB indicates N1.

questions.q: A 32-year-old presents with well-demarcated silvery scaly plaques on elbows, knees, and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. Histopathology shows elongated rete ridges with confluent parakeratosis and loss of granular layer. What cells are predominantly seen in the epidermis?
questions.exp: Psoriasis histology: acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, confluent parakeratosis, absent/reduced granular layer, suprapapillary plate thinning, dilated capillaries in papillary dermis, and Munro microabscesses (collections of neutrophils in stratum corneum). Auspitz sign (pin-point bleeding on scale removal) reflects dilated papillary capillaries.

questions.q: A 50-year-old is on systemic therapy for psoriasis. He develops oliguria, rising creatinine, and hypertension after 6 months. Renal biopsy shows afferent arteriolar hyalinization. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Cyclosporine nephrotoxicity is characterized by afferent arteriolar hyalinization, tubular atrophy, and interstitial fibrosis. It causes dose-dependent rise in creatinine and hypertension. The drug should be stopped if creatinine rises >25% above baseline. Maximum recommended duration is 1-2 years. Methotrexate causes hepatotoxicity/fibrosis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman is started on isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne. She must be counseled regarding teratogenicity. What is the recommended contraception protocol as per iPLEDGE program?
opts: One form of contraception starting 1 month before treatment
Two forms of contraception starting 1 month before, during, and 1 month after treatment
Oral contraceptive pills started 3 months after treatment ends
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (Category X). iPLEDGE requires TWO forms of contraception (one primary like OCP, one secondary like condom) starting 1 month BEFORE treatment, throughout treatment, and for 1 month AFTER stopping. Two negative pregnancy tests are needed before starting. Monthly monitoring is mandatory.

questions.q: A 25-year-old patient with recurrent genital herpes wants suppressive therapy. Which of the following is the correct dose of valacyclovir for suppressive therapy?
questions.exp: Valacyclovir for HSV suppression: 500mg once daily (1g once daily for patients with ≥10 recurrences/year or HIV-positive). Suppressive therapy reduces recurrence frequency, severity, and asymptomatic shedding (transmission risk). Episodic therapy dose is 500mg BD for 3-5 days or 1g OD for 5 days.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with hypopigmented macules on the face and neck. Wood's lamp examination shows ivory-white fluorescence. She has no sensory loss. KOH is negative. The macules are stable for 5 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Vitiligo shows bright chalk-white or ivory fluorescence under Wood's lamp (due to loss of melanin), making lesions more prominent and useful for detecting subclinical lesions. Pityriasis versicolor shows golden-yellow fluorescence. In leprosy, lesions are anesthetic. Wood's lamp highlights vitiligo lesions against surrounding tanned skin.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with itchy papules, vesicles, and excoriations involving the finger webs, wrists, and genital area. His roommate has similar complaints. Dermoscopy shows 'jet with contrail' sign. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Permethrin 5% cream applied from neck to toes for 8-12 hours
questions.exp: Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei) presents with intensely pruritic lesions in characteristic sites (interdigital spaces, wrists, genitalia). Dermoscopy shows 'delta-wing jet with contrail' pattern (the mite as the jet, burrow as contrail). First-line treatment: Permethrin 5% cream. Oral ivermectin is an alternative, especially for crusted (Norwegian) scabies. All contacts must be treated simultaneously.

questions.q: A 40-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 50 cells/μL) presents with large verrucous plaques on the face and neck. KOH mount shows large globose yeast cells with wide capsules. Mucicarmine stain is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cryptococcus neoformans in severely immunocompromised patients can present as molluscum contagiosum-like papules or verrucous plaques. The large encapsulated yeast stains with mucicarmine (capsule is mucicarminophilic). India ink prep shows the capsule as a clear halo. Cryptococcal skin lesions are a sign of disseminated disease.

questions.q: A 28-year-old presents with a linear, erythematous, serpiginous track on the dorsum of the foot that advances daily and is intensely pruritic. He recently returned from a beach vacation. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Cutaneous larva migrans (creeping eruption) is caused by hookworm larvae (Ancylostoma braziliense/caninum) penetrating skin on sandy beaches. The larvae migrate in the epidermis creating a characteristic serpiginous track. Treatment: oral ivermectin (200 mcg/kg single dose) or oral albendazole (400mg daily for 3-7 days). Thiabendazole topical is an older option.

questions.q: A 50-year-old presents with a painless ulcer on the sole of the foot with raised indurated edges. He has diabetes. The ulcer is surrounded by callus. Biopsy shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with large yeast cells showing broad-based budding. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Blastomycosis caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis shows thick-walled yeast with broad-based (single) budding on histology - this is the pathognomonic feature. Paracoccidioides shows multiple buds ('pilot wheel'). Histoplasma are tiny intracellular organisms. Blastomycosis primarily affects lungs but can disseminate to skin causing verrucous plaques or ulcers.

questions.q: During Mohs micrographic surgery for a recurrent BCC on the nose, the surgeon examines frozen sections showing positive margins on the lateral edge. What should be done next?
opts: Take another stage from the positive margin area only
Excise a wide 1cm margin from entire wound
Proceed with flap reconstruction and accept positive margins
questions.exp: Mohs surgery stages are performed sequentially. When margins are positive on a specific edge (lateral or deep), only that area is re-excised in the next stage, maximally preserving normal tissue. This targeted re-excision is repeated until all margins are clear. It allows highest cure rates (99% for primary BCC) with tissue conservation.

questions.q: A patient with extensive vitiligo on the face wants cosmetic improvement. He has stable vitiligo for 3 years. Topical steroids and PUVA have failed. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate for the face?
questions.exp: Non-cultured epidermal cell suspension (ReCell/melanocyte-keratinocyte transplant procedure) allows treatment of large areas with minimal donor site. It gives the best cosmetic results on the face with uniform repigmentation. It is ideal for larger areas. Suction blister grafting gives excellent color match but is limited to smaller areas. The condition must be stable (no progression for ≥1 year) before surgery.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with episodic painful ulcers in oral and genital mucosa recurring monthly, with associated hypopyon in the right eye. She is from Turkey. Pathergy test is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Behcet disease (more common in Silk Road countries including Turkey, Middle East) presents with recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis (hypopyon). Pathergy reaction (erythematous papule/pustule at needle prick site after 24-48h) is a characteristic feature. HLA-B51 is associated. Treatment: colchicine for mucocutaneous disease, azathioprine for eye disease.

questions.q: A 55-year-old presents with scarring alopecia. On scalp biopsy, there is a lymphocytic infiltrate around the infundibulum and isthmus destroying the sebaceous gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lichen planopilaris (LPP) shows lymphocytic infiltrate targeting the infundibulum and isthmus with destruction of sebaceous glands. The isthmus-targeting pattern is characteristic. Discoid lupus also causes scarring alopecia but shows perifollicular mucin deposition and interface changes. Frontal fibrosing alopecia is a variant of LPP affecting the hairline.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with yellow-brown discoloration of multiple fingernails with increased nail plate thickness and transverse ridging. She has a history of tinea unguium. KOH of nail clipping shows branching hyphae. What is the most effective treatment regimen?
opts: Topical amorolfine nail lacquer for 6 months
Oral itraconazole pulse therapy - 200mg BD for 1 week per month for 2 pulses
questions.exp: For fingernail onychomycosis, oral itraconazole pulse therapy (200mg BD for 1 week/month for 2 pulses) or continuous terbinafine (250mg daily for 6 weeks) are both effective. Terbinafine has the highest cure rate for dermatophyte onychomycosis. Itraconazole is preferred for Candida and non-dermatophyte onychomycosis. Toenails require 3-4 pulses of itraconazole or 12 weeks of terbinafine.

questions.q: A 35-year-old female presents with photosensitive rash, hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed areas, blistering, and hypertrichosis on the cheeks. Urine turns pink-red on standing. Urine shows increased porphyrins. LFTs are mildly elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) presents with photosensitive blistering (mechanobullous) on sun-exposed areas, milia, hypertrichosis (especially lateral cheeks), and skin fragility. Pink-red urine (due to uroporphyrin) under natural light and elevated urine uroporphyrins are characteristic. Associated with alcohol, hepatitis C, iron overload. Treatment: phlebotomy, hydroxychloroquine.
